Songs are revealing and personal — whether it’s a break-your-heart ballad (there are a few) or fantasy numbers to lift the mood...Be glad you didn’t live there. But this “Fun Home” is an unforgettable place to visit."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "How refreshing — a queer coming-of-age play in which the hero(ine) is not a diva, the parents are not monsters, and people are never mean, even when they’re being cruel. Lisa Kron’s warm, funny, heartbreaking book (from the graphic novel by Alison Bechdel) accomplishes all this without being sentimental.  That welcome tone of sincerity is replicated in her lyrics to Jeanine Tesori’s introspective songs, which sound like a human voice being painfully honest with itself."

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "Composer Jeanine Tesori and book writer/lyricist Lisa Kron tackle the material with great sensitivity and warmth. Their adaptation boasts a solid chamber-pop score, a handful of wonderful scenes and a winning cast.“Fun Home” has a lot going for it, thanks to the great affection and humor it accords its flawed, searching characters. Still, it’s ironic that a show about frustrated longings may leave you feeling the same."

criticReviews.author: Charles McNulty
criticReviews.excerpt: 'There have been plenty of new American musicals better put together than "Fun Home," but I can't think of one in recent years that has touched me as much with its tender, ironic and courageous vulnerability."

criticReviews.author: Elyse Sommer
criticReviews.excerpt: "Kron and Tesori have found an effective device to tell this sometimes funny but often painful coming of age story...Familiarity with the source is not needed to follow this musical version of the author-artist's journey to understanding herself and her father. It's not a journey geared to mass-market audiences, but one open-minded, adventurous musical theater lovers will not want to miss. "

criticReviews.author: Robert Kahn
criticReviews.excerpt: "The rich adaptation moves forward at a whirling pace...Tesori’s intricate melodies take hold from the opening. Kron’s book and lyrics hit the right notes of sensitivity and sarcasm...This is a father-daughter story, one that we know from its first moments will be tragicomic. “Fun Home” is a clear and pointed reminder that you’re not truly an adult until you’ve understood your parents as flawed human beings."

criticReviews.author: Chris Caggiano
criticReviews.excerpt: "Every once in a while, a musical comes along that restores my faith in the art form. 'Fun Home', is one of those musicals...if you haven't already seen 'Fun Home', you should. And if you have seen 'Fun Home,' you should go again...Lisa Kron and composer Jeanine Tesori have found just the right balance of humor and pathos to bring vivid life to Alison Bechdel's intensely moving graphic novel...The production is directed with both subtlety and bite by Sam Gold, and features an outstanding cast."

criticReviews.author: Mark Kennedy
criticReviews.excerpt: "A fresh musical that seems like an impossible sell on Broadway but hooks you instantly with its honesty and beauty. It is an adaptation from a graphic novel about growing up in a funeral home with a closeted gay dad. It should be theatrical suicide, and yet few shows are as moving, relatable and funny...Make sure 'Fun Home' is on your list."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "This story about a young woman coming to terms with her father’s probable suicide is suffused with death, not as a source of despair but of inspiration. The 2006 book exploded the possibilities of the graphic format. The musical by composer Jeanine Tesori and writer Lisa Kron -- with an enormous assist from Sam Gold’s inventive, sensitive staging -- lifts the story to a spectral plane without ever losing it's grounding."

criticReviews.author: Linda Winer
criticReviews.excerpt: "Extraordinary, disturbing and delightful...Based on Alison Bechdel's 2006 best-selling graphic memoir, this 100-minute treasure of invention captures the certainty and ambiguity of growing up in an amusing yet mysterious small-town Pennsylvania family."

criticReviews.author: Miriam Krule
criticReviews.excerpt: "While I’m a fan of musicals, this one, while at times a delight, has a difficult time living up to its source material...the graphic novel form allows for freedom from pesky constraints like linear time and geographical space; the theater, however, is less forgiving...Fun Home is not all longing and sadness; there are also moments of pure joy, and the musical shines during these...But aside from these few bright spots, it’s not clear that a musical is the best second format for the material."

criticReviews.author: Dana Piccoli
criticReviews.excerpt: "Overall,'Fun Home' is an unbelievable moving theatrical experience. It was one of the few times I’ve left a theatre lately feeling that I had been taken on a journey. I was never bored or distracted. Lesbian journeys are so rarely portrayed on the main stage. We are often relegated to the sidelines, indie festivals, and one-woman shows. 'Fun Home' takes Alison’s and our experience and gives it not only the validity that it deserves, but also a soundtrack to fill our hearts to the brim."

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "Beautiful: The Carole King Musical” should probably be titled “Brooklyn Girl.” This renaming would allow theatergoers to know exactly what to expect of the friendly, formulaic bio-musical."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Perhaps such material can’t be well directed, but we will never know. What I can say is that Marc Bruni certainly hasn’t improved it. The show is full of clunky transitions, dead space, scenes that peter out until someone mercifully snaps off the lights."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "King made magic with her catalogue and it is an unqualified treat to hear her best-known hits  performed live...Too bad a great musical isn’t only about the music. The book is crucial, too — and this show’s connect-the-dots story line is so simplistic that the extravagantly talented King’s life emerges as a mundane version of the long-suffering little woman."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "The early life and career of legendary singer-songwriter Carole King surely deserves more imaginative treatment than the corny chronological storytelling and old-fashioned musical format of “Beautiful.”  But all is forgiven, whenever Jessie Mueller, in the modest person of Carole King, sits down at the piano and pours heart and soul into familiar favorites from the composer’s songbook."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "McGrath, director Marc Bruni and the appealing performers don’t exactly break that mold by going for complexity. But while keeping things light and breezy, they have populated Beautiful with well-defined characters with relatable human foibles."

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "Watching Beautiful, the new jukebox musical celebrating the remarkable life and work of Carole King, you may not feel the earth move under your feet. But the new Broadway show emerges as a slick and joyous celebration of female empowerment."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "Director Marc Bruni has taken the gift of a smart and economical script and run with it. Amid lightning-quick transitions, this show only decelerates when it wants to. Split-second costume changes (designer Alejo Vietti must be a witch) add to the magic and fun of the evening."

criticReviews.author: Matthew Murray
criticReviews.excerpt: "Though Beautiful is ultra-slick and impeccably executed for what it is, electrifying it is not."

criticReviews.author: Michael Sommers
criticReviews.excerpt: “More than two dozen amazingly catchy songs of yesteryear are heard throughout ‘Beautiful’ as McGrath’s smart script nimbly relates how King, still in her teens, and Goffin, scarcely older, teamed up to turn out hits...What makes ‘Beautiful so, well, beautiful is watching King evolve from a dowdy, insecure teenager into a confident, mature artist...The show looks fresh in performance, thanks to a versatile, highly energetic ensemble.”

criticReviews.author: Melissa Rose Bernardo
criticReviews.excerpt: “The script is snappier than I remembered...Music-wise, the biggest thrill is hearing contrasting versions of songs you know and love...The switches between the writers’ and the pop stars’ renditions, thanks to director Marc Bruni, are quick and polished; and, even more important, the music, thanks to orchestrator/arranger Steve Sidwell, sounds dynamite...You’re bound to recognize all these songs...but please, for the sake of your fellow Carole King–loving audience members, don’t sing along."

criticReviews.author: Adrienne Urbanski
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Beautiful' places more focus on the music than the story and plot, making it not so much a tribute to Carole King’s life as it is a tribute to her large body of work...King’s relationship with Gerry is glossed over and we learn little about what their life is like. This leads to the end of their relationship feeling less dramatic and climactic than it could have been...Anyone who was not a fan of King’s songs before the show will most likely be one by curtain call."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: “Beautiful,” is beautifully performed and tuneful new entertainment.The story serves as an efficient delivery system for Carole King’s surprisingly diverse hits – not much more, nothing less."

criticReviews.author: Matthew Wexler
criticReviews.excerpt: "Director Marc Bruni and the design team keep things moving at a brisk pace. The show is tightly directed and seamlessly flows from the songwriters to the pop artists that shared their work with the world.  The hard-working ensemble takes on these musical icons, and while they look and sound incredibly polished, there is a decidedly “Broadway” sound to their vocal delivery."

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Beautiful' takes the early life story – and music – of the legendary singer-songwriter Carole King to create one of the most entertaining Broadway shows in years. All of the necessary elements have come together here, from a surprisingly smart and witty book by Douglas McGrath, smooth direction by Marc Bruni, and the work of a consistently top-notch cast. As a result, audiences leave with a song on their lips, a smile on their face, and even a tingle in their heart."

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: "Before we get to what's wrong with Beautiful: The Carole King Musical, let's establish what's so right that it instantly joins the ranks of irresistible jukebox tuners. In other words, it should have a long and healthy run, if, the producers can either convince Jessie Mueller to remain in the title role forever or if they can find replacements as enormously talented as she is."

criticReviews.author: Scott Harrah
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Beautiful' lacks the biographical wallop and dramatic intensity of such jukebox musicals as 'Jersey Boys' and the gleeful fun of 'Mamma Mia'... The presentation and performances of these venerable songs is hollow and spotty, like watching a highbrow version of TV’s 'Solid Gold'…Regardless, 'Beautiful' has a guilty-pleasure sense of fun and nostalgia and a few hearty performances, making us overlook the show’s many shortcomings."

criticReviews.author: Stu Brown
criticReviews.excerpt: "An entertaining blend of charm, nostalgia, and showmanship. The show’s overall feel and musicality will resonate greatly with a generation of baby boomers...While the book provides a cohesive plot and allows for a firmly developed point-counterpoint between the songwriting teams, the overall results for 'Beautiful' are problematic."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Spira
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s more of a living jukebox filled with Carole King’s works, with minimal context and a cringe-worthy Jewish mother added...The audience is there for the great music and choreography, and the cast does not disappoint...Unfortunately, some of the references will only make sense to AARP card-toting audience members...It’s practically a given that everyone will leave the show humming something from the Carole King catalog."

criticReviews.author: Perez Hilton
criticReviews.excerpt: "Beautiful lives up to its name and then some! The new musical based on the life of and featuring the music of legendary songwriter Carole King is a non-stop hit parade and the perfect example of a jukebox musical done right!"

criticReviews.author: Michael Higgins
criticReviews.excerpt: “Abby’s opening moment at the piano did lack the spark and charisma of Jessie–but once the actual story began, Abby pulled way ahead with her acting chops. She acted her way through each and every moment. I knew I was going to love the music, but this time I really connected with the character and her struggle. This show is so much more than just a jukebox collection of great songs. There is a wonderful story full of wit and pathos.”

criticReviews.author: Steve Parks
criticReviews.excerpt: "Jessie Mueller strikes a delicate balance between spunk and humility, making it impossible not to root for her as she morphs into an inspired Carole King."

criticReviews.author: Elysa Gardner
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mueller's portrayal of King — far and away the best reason to see Beautiful."

criticReviews.author: Robert Sholiton
criticReviews.excerpt: “Pretty much what I expected — a slick jukebox musical/biography of King’s early career...It is in very good shape. Although I had never heard of any of the present leads all were competent if not loaded with charisma...With 27 songs to squeeze in, there is no room in book for much more than connecting the dots...Bruni’s smooth direction keeps things moving...The singers were overamplified almost to the point of aural pain...If you like the music, you will probably have a good time.”

criticReviews.author: Erica Handel
criticReviews.excerpt: "From beginning to end, Baldwin beautifully sings Jason Robert Brown's score throughout the show...Lazar's intense and passionate portrayal of Robert made audiences root for him, even though his character was put into an awkward position...Baldwin and Lazar's scenes both together and apart were equally as incredible, showing how talented they truly are... Hunter Foster directs a production with excellent actors, beautiful music, and a story that will resonate with audiences for years to come. Anyone who has the opportunity to see this musical in person will love every minute of it."

criticReviews.author: Jay Lustig
criticReviews.excerpt: "Both sing beautifully, create fully rounded characters and project the urgent, larger-than-life emotions that Brown’s songs call for...This is a polished production, with strong performances throughout the cast...Hunter Foster, who played Bud in the 2014 Broadway production, directs. His deep familiarity with the material probably helped him draw out emotionally resonant performances from the cast members...The story’s melodrama is balanced by frequent reminders of the frustrating real-life challenges that Francesca and Robert face."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "The latest Broadway revival, which opened on Sunday at the Hudson Theater, goes wider, a notably rich and mostly successful approach."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Even after nearly three and a half hours of 'Death of a Salesman,' I'd gladly stay longer to watch that story continue."

criticReviews.author: Rob Weinert-Kendt
criticReviews.excerpt: It is not only the casting of the striving Lomans as a Black family that makes this Salesman a departure. It is also that the director, Miranda Cromwell, has rendered much of the play as a dissonant fever dream."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "Ms. Cromwell’s production is, nonetheless, emotionally wrenching as it digs fiercely into the heart of the play."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "The script is unchanged – and surprisingly accommodating to the fresh point of view...infusing the production with a legacy and identity all its own."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "Truly, it’s a rich and moving star performance and the reason to see the show."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s no doubt that casting a Black actor as Willy Loman (for the first time on Broadway, no less) adds a deeper dimension to this monumental role."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "The mournful irony Miller built into 'Death of a Salesman' is especially potent now, when our world so often feels as if it’s hanging by a thread. "

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "The climactic fight all the way to the inevitable conclusion is not affectingly tragic, and there is no build to speak of. Nice songs, but not enough attention was paid to the basics."

criticReviews.author: Lester Fabian Brathwaite
criticReviews.excerpt: "Maybe the enduring message of this production is that these themes are universal, that we all suffer the same under the yolk of The American Dream. And that, in spite of the odds, we all aspire to be great."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "73 years after it was written, 'Death of a Salesman' is still the great tragedy of our time."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: The best thing about Miranda Cromwell's sometimes uncertain production is the opportunity it gives four lead actors to do strong, stunning, and, in some cases, highly original work.

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "Wendell Pierce and Sharon D Clarke are giving extraordinary performances in a play that runs over three hours and that never lets up. The rest of the cast is also excellent...you are unlikely ever to see a finer production of Death of a Salesman than this one."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "In the hands of great lead actors, such as it is here, 'Death of a Salesman' still proves devastating with its Greek tragedy-like power."

criticReviews.author: Steven Suskin
criticReviews.excerpt: "Match a great play with great performers and a pitch-perfect production, and you are likely to leave the theatre in wonder at just what the playwright wrought."

criticReviews.author: Brittani Samuel
criticReviews.excerpt: "Not for one minute during the 190 of the current revival at the Hudson Theatre — where so much of Willy’s achingly complicated life is on display — did I feel nervous about his death."

criticReviews.author: Joseph Pisano
criticReviews.excerpt: To be clear, the casting isn't colorblind; it's just casting, with director Miranda Cromwell delicately drawing out a different set of lived experiences from Miller's almost untouched words. The play's West-End co-director Marianne Elliott has not  made the journey across the pond with its ongoing contributors, all of whom deserve kudos for the revelatory production, especially Wendell Pierce ("Broke-ology," "The Wire," "Treme") as Willy and Sharon D. Clarke ("Caroline, or Change") as Linda, his long-suffering wife. Though Pierce devastatingly pulls Willy apart in front of our eyes until all that's left is his sense of failure, it's Clarke who gives Willy's downfall its saddest dimension, convincing the audience, beyond any doubt, that the very-flawed Willy is loved.

criticReviews.author: Sarah Downs
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Death of a Salesman' on Broadway is epic...When you sit back at the final moment, the tide of emotion washing over you leaves you breathless. This is why we go to the theater."

criticReviews.author: Elyse Trevers
criticReviews.excerpt: "The play is still moving and engrossing and the main themes remain the same...Race adds another dimension to this new version of the 'Death of A Salesman,' a subtext while enhancing the bigger message."

criticReviews.author: Juliet Hindell
criticReviews.excerpt: "This 1949 play about a man confronting his failures and the failures of his family is also rendered new again through electrifying performances and inventive staging."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: These two formidable talents do give largely invigorating performances, and the recasting of the Lomans as a Black family certainly offers a fresh take on a play that’s been steadily produced since its much-acclaimed Broadway debut in 1949.  But for all the boldness of the reimagining, and the stellar track record of so much of the cast, “Death of a Salesman” is a disappointment in several ways.

criticReviews.author: Robert Hofler
criticReviews.excerpt: "Cromwell puts on quite a show. Sometimes it’s too much of a show."

criticReviews.author: Robert Hofler
criticReviews.excerpt: "Cromwell puts on quite a show. Sometimes it’s too much of a show."

criticReviews.author: Paulanne Simmons
criticReviews.excerpt: "This 'Death of a Salesman' may indeed be a crowd pleaser. Its humor makes the medicine go down quite smoothly, and the medicine is exactly the kind that makes us feel a lot better."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: “The play is thus less terrifying than teenifying — hence the plus sign instead of the ‘and’ in the title.”

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "By having a uniformly young cast, Romeo + Juliet successfully drives home the juvenile pettiness of the Montague/Capulet feud and sorrow...But this production of the love story hasn't quite found its heartbeat."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "What makes 'We Are Young' feel so right is more literal than all that: This Romeo and Juliet is very much about being young."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "...Sam Gold’s frenzied, youthful staging of the Shakespeare tragedy."

criticReviews.author: Trish Deitch
criticReviews.excerpt: "And the production is fun: The actors use the in-the-round theater to its fullest"

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "...director Sam Gold's hyperpop reimagining of 'Romeo + Juliet.'"

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "The enthusiasm is thrilling, even when it almost flattens you underfoot."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "During the dark final moments in the crypt...the play peters out."

criticReviews.author: Emlyn Travis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Kit Connor and Rachel Zegler are (violent) delights in Gen Z take on Shakespeare play"

criticReviews.author: Pete Hempstead
criticReviews.excerpt: "...this production is more for the kids"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “I'm afraid this Romeo and Juliet is a largely one-sided affair.”

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "...most-relatable entry level Shakespeare play to share with teenage students."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: "Sam Gold's youth-oriented reworking will please Gen Z more than their parents"

criticReviews.author: David Roberts
criticReviews.excerpt: "Their gender fluidity...embody the same characteristics in the tragedy itself."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: aimed unapologetically at Gen Z… sometimes the production thrilled…there are downsides

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: It’s hard to escape the feeling that the audience, regardless of age, is being patronized.

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "Kit Connor is a magnetic Romeo, projecting all the eagerness...of a charismatic young"

criticReviews.author: Deirdre Donovan
criticReviews.excerpt: Sam Gold’s revival is bound to appeal to Generation Z.

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: The love story marries theatre history with our present forms of entertainment.

criticReviews.author: Cary Wong
criticReviews.excerpt: A big welcome to what I’m dubbing Romeo + Juliet: The Jellicle Ball to Broadway.

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Spector’s hilarious poison-pen satire of educational wokeism has led us to that point with great care."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "But as both the comedy and the severity of the debate increase, the characters deepen beyond caricatures"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "A progressive school takes its mumps in Jonathan Spector's spiky comedy."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: “The show is a polite tiptoe along a cliff, a trek across a field of eggshells that as often as not are strewn atop landmines.”

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "play seems mostly to be a plea that we get better at accepting that humans are imperfect"

criticReviews.author: Daniel D'Addario
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Eureka Day' is a cleverly staged social satire, one that earns enough goodwill"

criticReviews.author: Harry Haun
criticReviews.excerpt: "started out a serious drama and acquired a lot of humor along the way"

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "...progressive politesse in shambles, profanity in all-caps, well-played emoji."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "produces plenty of laughter, but it’s hollow laughter of a certain type of righteousness"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "…it seems to encapsulate the last five years into a single explosive joke.”

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "Jonathan Spector's satirical dramedy...is a perfect reflection of our divisive times"

criticReviews.author: Joseph Pisano
criticReviews.excerpt: "both becoming exponentially more topical and more quaint over the last half decade or so"

criticReviews.author: David Roberts
criticReviews.excerpt: “...the cast brings authenticity and honesty to their complex characters."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "hilarious [but also] thought-provoking exploration of an alarmingly relevant issue"

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: It continues to excel as a bitingly topical dramedy.

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "Eureka Day‘s ending...offers a satisfying button on a well-crafted show."

criticReviews.author: Mark Rifkin
criticReviews.excerpt: "Jonathan Spector’s 'Eureka Day' is the funniest play of the season, striking gold again."

criticReviews.author: Cary Wong
criticReviews.excerpt: The acting ensemble is exceptional, with the always reliable Hecht particularly impressive

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: Exposes what happens when we let safety slide in favor of respecting beliefs.

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "For an elegantly vicious play that’s meant to draw pearls of blood, the actors, especially Cannavale and Harris, can come off as guarded, as if they’re fencing with blunted tips."

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Art' has humor, a wonderful cast, and the timeless clash of differing opinions. "

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Although 'Art' is not especially deep—Reza paints her characters in broad strokes but thin layers—it is solidly built for comedy, and all three men are armed with effective one-liners as their mutual exasperation builds to a climax. "

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "For all the play’s bickering and bashing, the eventual trajectory of Art feels almost saccharine."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Art drags a bit at the beginning – always has – but goes into hyperdrive with Corden’s scene-stealing rant about the horrors of a day spent planning a possibly ill-begotten wedding. "

criticReviews.author: Daniel D'Addario
criticReviews.excerpt: "The current Broadway climate has been thick on the ground with revivals of familiar titles anchored by big-name stars; the performances in 'Art”'..make the case for this as something more urgent than that."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Reza’s 1998 comedy abounds in witty chuckles and elegant structure, but it remains a slight boulevard comedy: three self-obsessed Frenchmen bickering over a pricey painting."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "Even though it turns into an indecipherable ramble midway through, the crowd applauded as if they’d just witnessed a Carpool Monologue. Unsurprisingly, the actor is highly watchable. Yet at Corden’s most entertaining, he’s his least connected."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "It makes the frothiest sex comedy from Broadway's postwar boom years look like Desire Under the Elms."

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: "...Reza has structured an intermissionless 90-minute tripart explosion of three men who have been friends for twenty-five years suddenly confronted with paying a bitter farewell to their apparently flimsy bonds."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "it delivers not only a very funny commentary on the pretensions of modern art but also a trenchant seriocomic look at the fragility of friendships and the machinations sometimes necessary to maintain them."

criticReviews.author: David Roberts
criticReviews.excerpt: “Yasmina Reza has successfully transformed the white Antrios painting into a trope, an extended metaphor for anything that stirs up uncomfortable and often destructive feelings between friends.”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Art" is not about art, and it’s not really about friendship. If it’s about anything at all, the Broadway revival of Yasmina Reza’s 30-year-old play is about the celebrity of Bobby Cannavale, James Corden and Neil Patrick Harris

criticReviews.author: Robert Hofler
criticReviews.excerpt: "After all the shouting and yelling in 'Art,' Reza glibly resolves the men’s differences in an epilogue that smacks of contrivance."

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: ‘Art’ is entertaining middlebrow fare, a kind of Gallic update of the urbane comedy of manners that Neil Simon mastered in an earlier era.

criticReviews.author: JK Clarke
criticReviews.excerpt: [Art] dead on arrival because the subject matter is no longer relevant.

criticReviews.author: Mark Kennedy
criticReviews.excerpt: "Under Scott Ellis’ tight and enthralling direction and with three perfectly cast actors...'Art' frequently erupts in laughter but still has plenty to say about friendship, power dynamics and how we get on each others’ nerves."

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: “a thoroughly engaging production of a whip-smart play”

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: Critic’s Pick:" 'Floyd Collins' reaches the sublime, and that is a rare achievement in any work of art."

criticReviews.author: Caroline Cao
criticReviews.excerpt: "Comedic quips keep the musical from sinking into bleakness, and Guettel’s folksy bluegrass score, complete with yodeling, is a remarkable one."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "The orchestra, directed and conducted by Ted Sperling, is superb; so is the full-bodied singing by Jordan as Floyd and McAlpine as Nellie. "

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "Floyd Collins leaves far too soft an impression. It never really joins its hero in the depths."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Floyd Collins' remains an intimate tale for such a large theater, although the space has its aptly cavernous aspects."

criticReviews.author: Christian Lewis
criticReviews.excerpt: "There may be treasure hidden deep in the cave that is “Floyd Collins,” but it may just be too dark and difficult to fully extract it. "

criticReviews.author: David Gordon
criticReviews.excerpt: "Floyd Collins is not a show for everyone—many will mistake its stillness for inertia, the use of negative space for emptiness—but if you surrender to the journey, you will feel everything."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "It's a strangely aloof piece, filled with ideas that need more flesh on their bones."

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "So, yes, there's a lot of cognitive dissonance we are asked to digest here. Yet, there is so much to both appreciate and enjoy...And Jeremy Jordan's performance alone is worth the price of admission."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: "never makes us feel what it is like to be plunged into total darkness"

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: Sonically spellbinding….It’s tempting to call this cave story shallow

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "The splashy and wonderfully sung revival of composer-lyricist Adam Guettel and writer-director Tina Landau’s 1996 musical Floyd Collins is an elegiac look at a uniquely American tragedy"

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: An incredible breath of fresh air.

criticReviews.author: Cary Wong
criticReviews.excerpt: An emotional and triumphant finale for both (Floyd) and the production.

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "This “Topdog/Underdog” is never in danger of being dragged down...The ending loses none of its explosive shock even if we’ve understood from the start that the odds in a hustle are always with the house."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "A massive Old Glory looms large and conveys a weighty sense of history. 'Topdog/Underdog' does that, too, in its own theatrical way. In this starry and stirring revival, the play unfurls in all its glory."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Superlative acting is at the core of the experience...Together, these two performers keep you guessing even as the play moves inexorably toward an outcome that has been in the cards all along."

criticReviews.author: Rob Weinert-Kendt
criticReviews.excerpt: "Afro-pessimism isn’t a genre in which I’d usually place Parks, let alone Leon. But played without winking in a key of aggrieved, stressed-out toxic masculinity, as it is here, 'Topdog/Underdog' is able to hit that note convincingly."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The characters’ passive complicity in their fates, and the play’s ultimate descent into violence, feels both simplistic and sensationalized. 'Topdog/Underdog' seems sadly retrograde."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Twenty years after it first arrived to shake up a complacent Broadway and make a Pulitzer Prize winner of its author Suzan-Lori Parks, 'Topdog/Underdog' has lost none of its vitality and power and cunning."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "All in all, this is really a show about how much we all need love, and to be loved. By our family, our friends and our country."

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "The first Broadway revival...crackles like a live wire — an American fable with its finger shoved in a socket. Throw in career-high performances from Corey Hawkins and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and it is a theatrical event in the most essential sense, in that it demands to be seen here and now."

criticReviews.author: Lovia Gyarkye
criticReviews.excerpt: "The confidence radiating from both [Lincoln and Booth] performances keeps 'Topdog/Underdog,' a play with a winking eagerness to elude meaning, light, electric and most of all funny."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "After an evening on Broadway with Corey Hawkins, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and the electrifying theatrical crossfire of 'Topdog/Underdog,' you’ll never again think of three-card monte as a mere money-grubbing street hustle."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "Director Kenny Leon has helmed a sharp, focused revival of the 2002 drama, with a pair of cracking performances that never let up."

criticReviews.author: Lester Fabian Brathwaite
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Top Dog/Underdog' is not a subtle play...If it were subtle, it would not be as watchable, or entertaining. And for a play that's just two characters monologuing or arguing, while dealing with some heavy issues — race, class, trauma, murder — Top Dog is pretty damn funny."

criticReviews.author: Matt Windman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Regardless, the production excels in the sharp and textured interplay between Abdul-Mateen and Hawkins, in which comedy-laced routines eventually culminate in showdown and tragedy."

criticReviews.author: David Gordon
criticReviews.excerpt: "What a thrill it is to be in the presence of Kenny Leon's new revival at the Golden Theatre, where two exciting actors — Corey Hawkins and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II — are picking up the cards and giving us a singular night of theater."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: Topdog/Underdog is a paradoxical proposition, a dead-end tale that nevertheless pulsates with humor and a kind of electric energy. Whatever happens to Booth and Lincoln, they aren't going quietly, and their creator provides them with plenty of furious life, making clear just how much humanity, informed by brains and talent, is going to waste

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Topdog/Underdog' manages to be both solidly realistic and as mythic as the story of the characters' historic namesakes that has long been embedded in the American consciousness."

criticReviews.author: Elyse Trevers
criticReviews.excerpt: "The dialogue is superbly written and moves very quickly. The performers are terrific and the play well worth seeing even though the subject is troubling."

criticReviews.author: Sandy MacDonald
criticReviews.excerpt: "It elicited a piercing collective scream on press night. You’ll need to be there yourself, on the edge of your seat, to feel the full impact."

criticReviews.author: Melissa Rose Bernardo
criticReviews.excerpt: "The dialogue between the two men positively crackles throughout, and the interplay between Abdul-Mateen and Hawkins—both edgy, raw, hilarious, and real—is razor-sharp."

criticReviews.author: Brittani Samuel
criticReviews.excerpt: "For all of the circularness of “Topdog/Underdog,” Leon does a great job of finding its dramatic points. With only two actors and a room, the play serves up a harsh account of the ills faced by America’s underdogs but does so with enough laughter to help the med-sin go down sweet."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: The 20th anniversary revival of Suzan-Lori Parks’ Pulitzer Prize-winning play, "Topdog/Underdog," is just as powerful and absorbing as before with its story of two African American brothers Booth and Lincoln who are searching for the American Dream in opposite ways. Under the astute but leisurely direction of Kenny Leon (Tony Award Best Revivals of "A Soldier’s Play," "A Raisin in the Sun" and "Fences"), rising stars Corey Hawkins (Tony nominated for "Six Degrees of Separation," and appearances in the film versions of "In the Heights" and "The Tragedy of Macbeth") and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II (Emmy Award winner for HBO’s "Watchmen" as well as ensemble awards for the cast of "The Trial of the Chicago 7") give riveted performances in this two-hander.

criticReviews.author: Holli Harms
criticReviews.excerpt: "They are not performing [Corey Hawkins and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II], they are inhabiting these amazing characters as they tear their way through the play, gnashing and gnawing, growling and harmonizing, running and crawling. They are breathtaking."

criticReviews.author: Elyse Trevers
criticReviews.excerpt: "The dialogue is superbly written and moves very quickly. The performers are terrific and the play well worth seeing even though the subject is troubling."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: The anachronism of the card game is not all that felt dated about this “Topdog/Underdog…[hile Kenny Leon’s direction highlights some comic moments and drives home some poignant ones – and Lord knows neither American violence nor Black despair are out-of-date — there is little in the current production that feels urgent.,,,  The play is less a literal depiction of two down-and-out Black brothers than a smart, dark, often funny allegory,

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: "Especially given the pair’s performances, we’d like to think these two men, despite the hands they’ve been dealt, will always have each other. But if we’re smart – and willing to read the clues Parks has given us – we know otherwise."

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "Both actors  [Corey Hawkins and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II] display an impressive physicality, commanding attention in long dialog-free scenes...right up to a final moment that still packs a punch even if you saw it coming from the show’s opening minutes."

criticReviews.author: Elysa Gardner
criticReviews.excerpt: "I attended a preview of Kenny Leon’s hilarious, harrowing new revival, in which every element, from the casting to the design, conspires to leave you shaken and stirred, and exuberantly entertained."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "In its remaking for Broadway I wish 'KPOP' had preserved more moments ... that allow you to consider what the excitement of K-pop (for those who feel it) and the expressiveness of American musical theater (likewise) can profitably say to each other."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Beyond the echo-chamber narrative, there’s much to like. There’s an irresistible cast of performers — 18 of them are making Broadway debuts — and attention-getting work by the design team that delivers the goods and then some."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Adapting 'KPOP' for Broadway was never going to be an easy task, and the effort to do so is commendable. But somewhere along its rise through the air, the musical’s bubble has burst. It’s just OKpop now."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s a lot in the musical 'KPOP' that makes for a successful show, including a winning ensemble, melodies that sneak into your ears and stay there, and rhythm-perfect choreography. But it has a curious inertia. It lacks drama."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: “ 'KPOP' felt like it was struggling to fulfill all the complex expectations it was facing, ironically a manifestation of its own internal themes."

criticReviews.author: A.D. Amorosi
criticReviews.excerpt: "The vulnerability behind what it takes to go big or go home is the secret, beating heart of 'KPOP,' a pulse that brings life to every chorus of its playlist."

criticReviews.author: Emlyn Travis
criticReviews.excerpt: "While the overall plot doesn't quite hit its mark, 'KPOP's' stellar musical numbers and all-star cast are able to turn the beat around into a solid, feel-good joyride that both K-Pop and musical fans can appreciate."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "There's not a weak link in the cast, which features some of the best vocalists and dancers on Broadway right now."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “It grieves me to say it, but KPOP has lost its pop -- also its snap and crackle. A critical and popular success five years ago in an immersive, walk-through production that was surely unsustainable for more than a limited run, it has been converted into a conventional book musical, in the process losing almost everything that made it distinctive. What's left are some kicky, if repetitive, tunes and shockingly slipshod dramaturgy. I cannot think of a show that, in its commercial transfer, has managed so thoroughly to shed so much of its stardust.”

criticReviews.author: James Wilson
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'KPOP' will not go down in the Broadway annals as a groundbreaking, or even a very good, musical. But when the company sings the final song, 'Blast Off,' you may realize that you're having too much fun to notice–or care."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'KPOP' certainly proves impressive on a technical level."

criticReviews.author: Brittani Samuel
criticReviews.excerpt: "Too much love and hard work envelops Bergman’s stage to not bop your head to the music or mimic dance moves from your seat."

criticReviews.author: Joseph Pisano
criticReviews.excerpt: Pardon the incredulity, but listening to a group of fresh-faced women sing "I only live to make you happy/anything you want just wind me up/and then I'll do it gladly" doesn't inspire confidence that South Korean popular music holds the key to universal well-being or should be regarded without moral reservation. Originally conceived off-Broadway as an immersive experience by playwright Jason Kim and the theater company Woodshed Collective, the first iteration of "KPOP" evinced its own nagging qualms about a star-making system comparable to the notorious old Hollywood one. But, in its journey to Midtown, a reimagined "KPOP" has abandoned its weightier self-awareness, along with a lot of its creativity.

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: The new premise pretends that an American filmmaker...is filming a documentary,..When the music—mostly power-blasting, heavily rhythmic explosions...—stops, so, basically, does the show so we can sit through flatlining soap-operatics.

criticReviews.author: Victoria Dammer
criticReviews.excerpt: "The ending dance finale, where both groups combined in one incredible performance, brought the noise level to a crescendo rarely heard on Broadway. It was more like a concert, and those in attendance were sorry the show was over so quickly."

criticReviews.author: Loren Noveck
criticReviews.excerpt: "The production numbers bring the house down, but there’s not much else there."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: I loved “KPOP” when I saw it five years ago Off Broadway,  but the “KPOP” on Broadway is not the same show ….  It’s still exciting, sometimes thrilling -- but it's a packaged entertainment rather than an adventure in theater.… a K-pop concert….  The stories are presented awkwardly and mostly feel like filler between the musical productions.

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: "Admittedly, Helen Park and Max Vernon’s all-original score, performed in a mix of Korean and English, bears very little connection to the show’s flimsy plot and doesn’t make much of an emotional impact."

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "The concert-style show has a pulsing energy but not much plot."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: “That we see these options so starkly is because everything else is pared away. Herzog’s dialogue, pruning the social floweriness and conversational whorls of Ibsen’s naturalism, gets right to the point of every line, leaving the text raw and red, as if exfoliated."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: “The new Broadway production of Henrik Ibsen’s ‘A Doll’s House’ starring Jessica Chastain is laser-focused, laid bare, and simply stunning. “

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "The superb Jessica Chastain plays Nora Helmer ... and Jamie Lloyd’s staging zeroes in on her with relentless focus."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “It all ends up making this production of ‘A Doll’s House’ feel like an exercise that acting students might do to get a better bearing on their characters”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “In scrubbing away virtually all action and much interaction from the play, Mr. Lloyd reduces its power to move us to reflection and feeling. We are left with a skeleton of this still-vital play, all bones, no flesh.”

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Anyone willing to give in to the wily charms and stealthy spell of this stark, thoughtful production will find a singular Broadway experience, a smart and captivating experiment in the power of the voice to transport us to places both far away and deep inside the human psyche."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "If you are a fan of Chastain’s work, this is not something to miss, if only to watch how she builds outwards from inside a theatrical, and marital, box."

criticReviews.author: Trish Deitch
criticReviews.excerpt: "In this revival, what’s left is a beautiful, spacious clarity about what this oft-produced play is about, who these characters are, what they mean to one another and how they may (or may not) impact audiences of today.

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘A Doll’s House’ was considered shocking in its day for showing Nora’s rejection of that trap. When she steps out of the Helmer home and quite literally into the 21st century in this boldly conceived, commandingly acted production, it’s both shattering and exhilarating.”

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: “If comedy is a play that ends in a wedding, then ‘A Doll’s House’ is a comedy that ends in divorce.”

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘A Doll’s House’ is concerned almost as much with money as it is with freedom...The notion of women understanding their own power and rejecting being controlled (and worse) by men remains remarkably topical.”

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: “Call me old fashioned, but to take a play about a woman who powerfully realizes she’s not just a plaything for men, but her own human being, and end it with a cutesy gimmick is wrongheaded. It’s another silly toy in the dollhouse.”

criticReviews.author: Leah Greenblatt
criticReviews.excerpt: "The Oscar winner [Jessica Chastain] takes on a bare-bones modernization of Henrik Ibsen's classic play, to mixed results."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “When acted as well as it is here, ‘A Doll's House’ remains indestructible, resilient in the face of directorial gimmicks.”

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “It's the first time, in my experience, that ’A Doll's House’ overstays its welcome. Call it creaky but, handled with care, it bristles with life; here, it seems to be looking for a place to lie down.”

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: “Many undoubtedly will want to attend ‘A Doll's House’ in order to see Jessica Chastain's performance...Regardless, it is difficult to avoid feeling overwhelmed by the heavy-handedness of the production.”

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: “The stunt completely takes you out of the play and leaves you thinking not about the epochal nature of Nora’s decision but rather the director’s ingenuity in pulling it off. Which, I suspect, is exactly how he likes it.”

criticReviews.author: Steven Suskin
criticReviews.excerpt: “Herzog has trimmed the play of excessive dramaturgy without losing Ibsen’s effectiveness, handily getting us out of the theatre in less than two hours instead of what typically approaches three. “

criticReviews.author: Brittani Samuel
criticReviews.excerpt: "In this boldly envisioned, yet minimalistically executed production directed by Jamie Lloyd and adapted by Amy Herzog, silence and simplicity are constantly at play."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: Like Ivo van Hove’s pared-down revival of Arthur Miller’s "A View from the Bridge," Jamie Lloyd’s new Broadway production of Henrik Ibsen’s 1879 "A Doll’s House" uses no sets or props and all black costumes for the entire cast. Going even further than van Hove, he has the heroine Nora Helmer played by film star Jessica Chastain seated almost for the entire length of this intermission-less three-act play. Using a new version by Amy Herzog recast in spare modern vernacular, this "Doll’s House" proves to be riveting and intense, even if you know the play very well, focusing our attention on the dialogue, the acting and emotion, rather than the décor and the historical trappings of 19th century Norway as we usually do.

criticReviews.author: Carol Rocamora
criticReviews.excerpt: “Lloyd’s bold, fearless directorial choices emphasize the timelessness of Ibsen’s play—as the author must have hoped for...Ibsen is timeless—he doesn’t need to be updated, only translated.”

criticReviews.author: Tulis McCall
criticReviews.excerpt: “When Nora finally stands up on her own two feet, when she gives the final final, it feels as if we have all been given permission to breathe, and, if we choose, permission to walk out into the world by her side. Remarkable.”

criticReviews.author: Elyse Trevers
criticReviews.excerpt: “I found ‘A Doll’s House’ slow and didactic. The ending felt more preachy. Although Herzog’s version is creative and modern, the pared-down play doesn’t do the subject matter justice. The actors work hard but they need more; unfortunately, here they got less.”

criticReviews.author: Lane Williamson
criticReviews.excerpt: “There’s so much to appreciate in this revival, particularly Herzog’s writing and the scenework between Chastain and Moayed.”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: It’s too tempting to mock this austere version of Ibsen’s play as Broadway’s answer to the movie that just swept the Oscars. Call it: Nothing Nowhere With No Intermission!... Yet…there are two main reasons I was happy to have attended director Jamie Lloyd’s often off-putting production — playwright Amy Herzog’s refreshingly idiomatic rewrite of the usual stodgy translations from Ibsen’s Norwegian, and Jessica Chastain’s performance in the last fifteen minutes

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: “Words definitely speak louder than actions in Jamie Lloyd’s much-anticipated revival of Henrik Ibsen’s landmark 1879 play “A Doll’s House.’ ”

criticReviews.author: Darryl Reilly
criticReviews.excerpt: Jessica Chastain’s awesome performance as Nora, director Jamie Lloyd’s vivid modern production, Amy Herzog’s pointed adaptation and a coup de théâtre finale, all make this stripped-down revival of Henrik Ibsen’s A Doll’s House a stimulating and memorable theatrical event.

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: Chastain’s performance is superbly constructed, the cracks in its veneer sometimes visible but, until there’s no recourse, never threatening to bring the structure down. When Nora finally succumbs, she does so with deep power mingled with restraint...Ms. Chastain...has met the role’s challenges and left her indelible mark on it.

criticReviews.author: David Sheward
criticReviews.excerpt: “There are no spoilers here, but suffice it to say that the finale of this inventive revival is as theatrical and surprising as all that precedes it. This is a very sturdy, although unfurnished ‘Doll’s House.’ ”

criticReviews.author: Benjamin Lindsay
criticReviews.excerpt: "Other than the music and Chastain’s extremely emotive performance, Jamie Lloyd’s direction is a parody of minimalism in the theater."

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: “If ‘Summer, 1976’ feels too comfortable to be fashionable, it’s sharply observant, too, and subtly, insistently feminist — more than the wisp of a two-hander that it might first appear to be.”

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: “...’Summer, 1976,’ a pleasant wisp of a play with an A-list pedigree that has all the dramatic heft of catching a few rays...this new work provides a not-so-surprising reminder about a simple fact of life. People come into our lives and then they go, but they leave a mark – whether we want to acknowledge that or not.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “I don’t regret the 90 minutes I spent at this smoothly rendered memory play. But already, I struggle a bit to remember it. ”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “They don’t experience anything grandly triumphant or devastating, but the play offers the challenge of sitting quietly, meeting them at their level, and considering what is big from that vantage.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “...the play is small in scale—just two characters, coming in at 90 minutes—unusual in its design, and filled with interesting detail. The closer you look, and listen, and the more you reflect upon it, the deeper grow its rewards.”

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: “Broadway can be a loud place, with belters belting and orchestras swelling and actors playing to rafters in the theater across the street, so it’s both comforting and mesmerizing to see a play as quietly poignant as David Auburn’s ’Summer, 1976.’ ”

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: “It breaks some of the spell of empathy and shared experience, which may well have been fully intentional. A tilt toward a crucial spark, then, but not as helpful as really catching summer heat.”

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: “There’s not one false note in director Daniel Sullivan’s clear direction or in the natural yet precise performances of Linney and Hecht, who are working at the top of their game and together offer a master class in acting.”

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: “Auburn’s play is told mostly in monologues to the audience — only rarely do the two speak directly to each other or embody another character. And only a few major events happen over 90 minutes.”

criticReviews.author: Dalton Ross
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ...‘Summer, 1976’ highlights how simpler moments and interactions along one's timeline can still have a profound and long-lasting impact — much like the play itself.”

criticReviews.author: Christian Lewis
criticReviews.excerpt: “Watching Linney and Hecht’s extremely grounded performances, you will inevitably be reminded of your own friendships, current and former...Because of that, ’Summer, 1976’ is a must-see–a rare perfect play with two brilliant performances at the center. ”

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “It's a measure of the care with which Summer, 1976 has been written, produced, and performed that, days later, you may find yourself musing about Diana and Alice -- their impact on each other and the way small decisions can send lives veering in unexpected directions. Some friendships last a lifetime; others barely survive a season. But who's to say which is more important?”

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: “...’Summer, 1976’ comes off as a literary exercise, an enacted short story about a series of situational connections with others that happen to most of us most of the time.”

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: “The play nonetheless proves affecting, thanks to its sensitive insights about the vagaries of friendships and the way they can evolve, or not, with the passage of time and the impact of external forces. ”

criticReviews.author: Sandy MacDonald
criticReviews.excerpt: “The production itself is flawless...Director Daniel Sullivan deftly delineates every interaction – subdued to explosive.”

criticReviews.author: Brittani Samuel
criticReviews.excerpt: “For a show that prides itself on being an insightful examination of female friendship, ‘Summer, 1976’ rarely goes beyond the surface of its central one.”

criticReviews.author: Joel Benjamin
criticReviews.excerpt: A world premiere production of the Manhattan Theatre Club at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, Summer, 1976 has been directed by Daniel Sullivan whose nuanced approach turns Auburn’s words into three-dimensional portraits.  Under his guidance two brilliant artists slowly reveal layers of emotion, turning what might have been an unoriginal premise into a rich tapestry.

criticReviews.author: Carol Rocamora
criticReviews.excerpt: “Auburn’s dialogue flows smoothly, naturally, and artfully—from direct audience address to conversation between Diana and Alice and then back to audience address. It’s delivered with command and panache by these two virtuosic performers, Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht.”

criticReviews.author: David Walters
criticReviews.excerpt: “...a comfortable play, but raised in stature by the acting prowess of its two stars, Jessica Hecht and Laura Linney, and by the shape-shifting translucence of the set by John Lee Beatty, and subtly participatory lighting of Japhy Weideman.”

criticReviews.author: Cameron Kelsall
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Summer, 1976’ could certainly find something interesting to say about female friendship, bonds of necessity, and cultural currency. But at present, it feels like a star vehicle hastily slapped together, promising much and delivering little. ”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht sit at the same table but don’t look at one another, nor talk to each other, at the beginning of this exquisitely acted production of David Auburn’s gauzy, bittersweet, and  largely inert new play….“Summer, 1976” has the modest lyricism of a short story, albeit one voiced by world-class actresses. It’s no surprise that Audible is planning to release a recording of it as an audiobook.

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: “While brilliantly acted by Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht, the 90-minute play ultimately feels like a stretched-out anecdote. We wait for an exciting plot twist, but two arrive that turn out to be dream sequences, while another struck me as less-than-believable.”

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: “The play is a sweet time-passer of no particular theatrical importance, delightfully acted, directed, and designed, with moments of laughter and pathos coated in a light glaze of nostalgia.”

criticReviews.author: Robert Hofler
criticReviews.excerpt: “...director Daniel Sullivan delivers a far greater theatrical spectacle with Linney and Hecht attempting to communicate at often cross purposes for 90 minutes. His coordination of the technical elements is equally arresting.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "NYTImes Critic's Pick! The wonder is that it is never less than thrilling to experience. This being a musical, the music is part of that; Tesori’s wondrous score is like the search function on a car radio, picking up snippets of every genre on the dial...Clarke, who won an Olivier award for her performance in the British production, adds hers. She makes of the maid an almost Shakespearean figure; even at the depths of the character’s despair."

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Some performances tell an entire story unto themselves. Sharon D Clarke delivers one such stunning star turn in this revival of Caroline, or Change, propelled onto Broadway by her acclaim in its previous London run. With an earth- and rafter-trembling embodiment of the title character, Clarke animates a curious — and at times troubling — musical with undeniable life."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Directed by Michael Longhurst with intensity and sensitivity, and performed by a cast that seems to have made a pact to sustain itself at the towering heights achieved early and unfailingly by its mighty star Sharon D Clarke, this Caroline, Or Change is a hurricane wind unleashed on decrepit legacies and newfound cautions."

criticReviews.author: Ayanna Prescod
criticReviews.excerpt: "All of these story elements spun together wrestle with issues that are still urgent today. As one memorable lyric in the show states, there is “no underground in Louisiana.” But on the surface in New York City, there is an important musical revival on Broadway that is deeply meaningful, crucial to experience and definitely a necessary change."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "The same text by librettist and lyricist Tony Kushner, which had seemed so stiffly fragmented in that earlier production, finds a fluid cohesion here that makes not only Caroline’s solitude, but the isolation of almost everyone around her profoundly affecting...Anyone who has missed the overwhelming emotional power of a great Broadway musical in the past 19 months should look no further."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "Clarke is strong in a role that’s damn tough...Of course, Kushner and Tesori’s show has always been a pompous slip of a thing that’s rather high on itself. There are no melodies to speak of, and the whole score sounds like a wind chime."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: Caroline, or Change has often been acclaimed -- for its powerful central characterization and for a score that melds the blues, klezmer, soul, and '60s pop sounds to powerful effect -- but it is a singular, indeed eccentric, piece that is not for all tastes. See it for Clarke; who knows when she will come our way again?

criticReviews.author: Steven Suskin
criticReviews.excerpt: "Sharon D Clarke doesn’t quite take the stage of Studio 54, mind you. She is cemented to it...Clarke—who has thus far been a remarkable, intensely controlled presence—breaks through with a searing intensity most welcome after the recent series of societal upheavals. Some of which, mind you, are especially relevant to the theme and content of Caroline, or Change."

criticReviews.author: Elysa Gardner
criticReviews.excerpt: "If there are a few slow-moving moments in Longhurst’s production, the payoff is big; it’s unlikely that anyone with a beating heart will leave after Act Two without moist eyes, or at least a lump in the throat...It’s not easy to juggle despair and exuberance without resorting to sentimentality, and Caroline still manages the task handily."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "Clarke imbues the character with a quiet but smoldering intensity that galvanizes the musical into vivid, almost nerve-rattling life whenever she is center stage...for this viewer, it is the unblinking yet compassionate portrait of the title character that lifts the show into the sublime, and Clarke’s performance — much like Tonya Pinkins’s in the original production — is the driving force behind its moments of transcendence."

criticReviews.author: Joel Benjamin
criticReviews.excerpt: "To be sure, Sharon D Clarke (London’s Olivier Award for Best Actress in a Musical, 2019) gives a jolting, heartbreaking performance in the title role, but has a coldness that never melts, even in her scenes with her family (until the very end).  She roars through her long, heartbreaking solo towards the end bringing the house down."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Sharon D Clarke sings a breathtaking 11 o’clock number ...my enthusiasm for this first Broadway revival of Tony Kushner and Jeanine Tesori’s inventive, thoughtful and affecting collaboration comes not just from those aspects of the show that satisfy audience expectations about big Broadway musicals.  What makes this work so powerful, and especially timely, is how this splendid cast tells a small story about change – literal pocket change – while offering a larger glimpse into the complex undercurrents in a tense moment of change in American history."

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: “Too much of the insistently rhythmic music lacks variety, the best moments coming in the klezmer sequence and in Clarke’s tear-down-the-house, eleven o’clock number, “Lot’s Wife”… Still, this isn’t a show with takeaway songs. Caroline, or Change’s two hours and 15 minutes are overlong, but by the time it ends, you’ll understand why it’s here and why now couldn’t be a better time to have it around.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Though sometimes mesmerizing, “Flying Over Sunset,” the new musical about LSD that opened there on Monday, is mostly bewildering, and further proof that transcendence can’t be shared."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "The production is a head-scratcher from the get-go as the ensemble parades single file, doing loop-de-loops around the stage. Footsteps are loudly amplified, presumably to suggest the heightened sensory impact of LSD, but who knows. What’s clear is that the actors go in circles and so does the show. The second half restates what’s already been said in the first act, but with splashier visual effects. Songs drift in and out, etching vaporous impressions while they’re at it. The pretty title song emerges as the most vivid."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "The Lincoln Center production has real pleasures: Yazbeck shares a thrilling music-hall duet, choreographed by Michelle Dorrance, with his younger self (Atticus Ware), who is dressed as a girl; Cusack sings as beautifully as always, as does Laura Shoop as Huxley’s wife. And the staging is very handsome indeed: Beowulf Boritt’s expansive set, Toni-Leslie James’s costumes and Bradley King’s lighting are all first-class. But these elements can only distract so much from a show that would probably make more sense as a one-act in a smaller space. What a long, strange trip it is."

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "The image does not set up a theme or a motif or illuminate some unseen truth. The show’s songs — lush but dull music by Kitt, lyrics by Korie — all show us acid trips, yet the grindingly inert and ineffectual Judith number makes you keen never to share one of these hallucinations again."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Overlong and occasionally (but only occasionally) a bit tedious, the last third of the show loses its way. There’s some Freudian demon-facing, a lot of long-delayed (and fairly pat) self-acceptance and, in the case of the short-shrifted Gerald, a bit of ascendant fighting spirit, but for all the talk of communal experience and shared enlightenment, Flying Over Sunset just can’t quite figure out what these characters ultimately mean to, or do for, one another."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "the creatives of this delectable theatrical bonbon treat us to a tasteful trip on the mild side...The show’s trippy sensibility is strikingly displayed on Beowulf Boritt’s spare, highly stylized cycloramic set and under Bradley King’s luscious lighting, which turns the color blue into a juicy fruit so cool and sweet the eye can almost taste it. Mixing up the senses is very much a quality of this thoughtful and unusually literate musical, which book writer and director Lapine has apparently conceived as a head trip with brains."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt:
"This offbeat premise — smartly realized only by Beowulf Boritt’s scenic designs and the projections by 59 Productions — has been turned into an entertainment about as scintillating as an Agriculture Department instructional video on crop irrigation. It’s as if Lincoln Center Theater and the accomplished creative team (with two Pulitzer Prizes among them) came to the creative juncture of delightful and tedious and took the wrong fork.

Long-winded and impossibly earnest, the world-premiere musical, which marked its official opening Monday night at the Vivian Beaumont Theater, features an unremarkable score by Tom Kitt and Michael Korie and a lumbering book by James Lapine, who also directs."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt:
"Being the only sober person in a room full of drunks is never any fun. Neither, as it would happen, is being an audience member at a musical about rich people who are high on LSD.

At least its trippy cousin “Hair” has energetic songs and some cute hippies who jump around to them."

criticReviews.author: Matt Windman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Unfortunately, “Flying Over Sunset” is an artistic misfire – and a nearly three-hour slog to sit through. The book is devoid of conflict (relying instead of introspection and confession), expository (filling in details about the politics of the period), repetitive (with the second act more or less mirroring the first act), and indulgently weird...With the exception of the evocative title song (which is powerfully performed by Cusack), the ethereal score is weighed down by prosaic lyrics and a lack of melody."

criticReviews.author: David Gordon
criticReviews.excerpt: "While I'll give Flying Over Sunset some well-earned points for its originality (the theatrical equivalent of an A for effort, I guess, but that and a dollar will get you on the subway), the show ultimately commits the cardinal sin of entertainment: It's just boring. There are people who will get more out of this abstract musical about grief than I did, and I hope they do."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: Flying Over Sunset just might be the best anti-drug PSA ever. Show it to young people thinking about getting high and I'll bet they'll swear off the stuff for life. They won't be scared straight, mind you; they'll just wonder what the fuss is all about. Among the new musical's many assets are a daringly original premise, a stellar trio of leads, some lovely melodies, and a stunning production design that uncannily mirrors its characters' stream-of-consciousness moments. But an abundance of interesting ideas never coalesces into the hallucinatory, revelatory experience the show seems to promise.

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show’s attempts at surrealist flights of fancy prove more cringeworthy than transporting...The performers do everything possible with their characters, especially the luminous Cusack, but they’re ultimately undone by the material, which includes Sella being reduced to doing a pratfall and planting his face in Yazbeck’s posterior for a cheap laugh. And why the talented Yazbeck doesn’t even make an attempt at impersonating Grant’s distinctive Mid-Atlantic accent is a question best left unasked."

criticReviews.author: Elysa Gardner
criticReviews.excerpt: "the production is aesthetically transcendent—a sensory feast for the sober that never settles for gratuitous flash, and is as pleasing to listen to as it is to behold. Kitt provides some of his most melodically and harmonically satisfying work to date, and the material is beautifully sung"

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "ambitious and frequently moving...While this adventurous journey into the psyches of celebrities on psychedelics has its longueurs, the score, with music by Tom Kitt (“Next to Normal”) and lyrics by Michael Korie (“Grey Gardens”), and the book and direction by James Lapine, are as accomplished as one would expect from such talents. And the production, from Lincoln Center Theater, is ravishingly beautiful, as this deep-pocketed company bravely puts it ample resources behind this decidedly unlikely project."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt:
Flying Over Sunset, Pulitzer Prize-winning bookwriter/director James Lapine’s new original show, is a “What If?” musical: using historical facts that are known about writer and philosopher Aldous Huxley, politician and diplomat Claire Boothe Luce, and actor and film star Cary Grant, he has created a fictitious story about their experimenting with LSD together in the late 1950’s. 

The problem seems to be that Lapine doesn’t appear to know much about them so that the results are extremely thin though the musical still manages to run a little under three hours. The songs by Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Tom Kitt and lyricist Michael Korie don’t add a great deal and the production design which ought to be psychedelic is subdued and unadventurous. Stars Harry Hadden-Paton as Huxley, Carmen Cusack as Luce and Tony Yazbeck as Grant try valiantly but they can’t breathe life into generic cardboard cutouts.

criticReviews.author: Stanford Friedman
criticReviews.excerpt: "the result is a long, not strange enough trip with as many faults as there are stellar components. The production features the best tap dance solo to be found on Broadway, but Michelle Dorrance’s choreography otherwise, while of a singular vision, feels out of step with the gliding pace of the show established by director James Lapine. There are ravishing sets by the brilliant Beowulf Boritt, clever costumes (Toni-Leslie James) and strong performances throughout, but they are in service of music by Tom Kitt that is lilting to the point of stifling, and a book by Lapine so overloaded with biography and exposition that it is no wonder its characters are seeking escape."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: There are certainly some highlights in “Flying Over Sunset,” chief among them Tony Yazbeck’s phenomenal dancing as Cary Grant...However, after sitting through the nearly three hours of this unique fusion of high-minded spiritual contemplation, gossipy biographical tidbits, subtle comedy and fabricated hallucinations all presented in song and dance, I was never completely persuaded that these three famous figures belong in the same musical

criticReviews.author: Robert Hofler
criticReviews.excerpt: "Regardless of who’s singing, as soon as the vocals start, the massive set (by Beowulf Boritt) changes shape to reflect hallucinatory projections (by 59 Productions) that visualize what the characters are now experiencing in their head; colors intensify and the physical world drops away. Lapine also directs, and he handles the many elements like a master general. Fortunately, nobody gets swept into the orchestra pit by Boritt’s big, moving set."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "When 'American Buffalo' first hit the stage, in Chicago in 1975, its portrait of lowlifes like Teach — two-bit grifters aping the realpolitik of American business — was a game changer. Though it did not quite induce sympathy for a man who would strike a kid in the face with an iron, it did make audiences queasy about the respectable entrepreneurs whose behavior Teach was translating to his own turf. In language as crass and cadenced as gunfire, Mamet turned their man-eat-man philosophy, which some call capitalism, into brutal prole poetry: a poetry of predation, you might even say."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Directed by Neil Pepe with the expert eye for appraisal that the characters lack, this production is vastly superior to 'American Buffalo’s' last Broadway incarnation, which ran briefly back in 2008. The play itself, which marked Mamet’s breakthrough, is as thin as a dime, but it’s got great atmospherics. Scott Pask’s set and Dede Ayite’s costumes plunge us into the shabby world of the action; seated around the thrust stage at Circle in the Square, the audience can almost smell the mix of dirt and desperation. "
